title: Multiscale Chemistry and Structure of Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease Lesions
content: Scleractinian corals protect their soft polyps by building an exoskeleton from aragonite, a highly ordered polymorph of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) [1]. In hierarchically organized corallites, aligned single-crystalline aragonite fibers extend radially about nucleation sites in a process termed spherulitic growth [2]. These nucleation sites are called centers of calcification (COC), which contain clusters of amorphous calcium carbonate (ACC) precursor [3, 4]. Studies have shown that the crystal growth process in many species of hard corals, including Montastraea cavernosa, begins with the attachment of biogenic amorphous calcium carbonate (ACC) precursor particles at the centers of calcification [5]​. Corals have been described as mesocrystals, meaning nanodomains with small misorientations are hierarchically organized into mesostructures [6]. The mineralization process of healthy coral skeletons has been studied extensively, but while many aspects of nucleation and growth are not yet fully understood, even less is known about the effect of diseases on the mineralized skeleton.
